title: Pontic Greek (Romeyka): the Black Sea dialect
lead: Pontic Greek was spoken along the south-eastern coast of the Black Sea, the ancient **Πόντος**, in some 800 towns and villages stretching about 400 km from İnebolu in the west to the edge of Georgia in the east, and up to 100 km inland. Its speakers called it **Ρωμαίικα** ('Roman', i.e. Byzantine Greek), sometimes **Λαζικά**; Greeks today call it **Ποντιακά**. After 1923 almost all its Christian speakers came to Greece, where Pontic is still the most widely spoken of the strongly divergent dialects, kept alive in families, music and dance. A Muslim variety, Romeyka, survives in the valleys east of Trabzon.
facts: Historically the Pontus (Trabzon, Of, Sürmene, Giresun, Samsun, the mining district of Gümüşhane/Argyroupolis); after 1923 mainly Macedonia, Thrace and Attica. Earlier migrations to Georgia, southern Russia (Stavropol, Krasnodar) and Ukraine.

Estimates for Greece range from about 200,000 to 400,000 people with some knowledge, most of them bilingual and many second-generation; a few thousand Romeyka speakers in Turkey (estimates vary widely).
No official status in Greece. UNESCO: 'definitely endangered'.
Hellenistic Koine of Asia Minor, isolated from the 7th–8th c. on; independent Empire of Trebizond 1204–1461.

**Τραπεζουντιακά** (Trebizond, Matsouka, Santa, Chaldia, Of), **Οινουντιακά** (Oinoe/Ünye, closer to the standard), **Χαλδιώτικα** (inland, more Turkish influence). Mariupolitan (**Ρουμέικα**) in Ukraine descends from the related Crimean Greek.
Greek alphabet with extra marks: **σ̌, ζ̌, ξ̌, ψ̌** for [ʃ ʒ kʃ pʃ] and **α̈, ο̈** for [æ ø]; Latin letters in Turkey, Cyrillic in the former USSR.

timeline.text: Ionian Greeks from Miletus and its colony Sinope found trading towns on the southern Black Sea coast, among them **Τραπεζούς** (Trabzon).
The Koine spreads inland. Pontic, like other Asia Minor varieties, grows out of the local Koine, not out of ancient Ionic.
Arab invasions and a frontier way of life cut the Pontus off from the Greek west. Scholars place the start of Pontic's divergence here.
The **Empire of Trebizond** under the Grand Komnenoi, independent of Constantinople. No Pontic texts survive; the dialect was oral.

Ottoman rule. In the 17th–19th c. many villages of the **Of** valley convert to Islam but keep their Greek. From the 18th c. many Christians move to the Russian Empire (Georgia, the Caucasus, southern Russia).
Deportations and massacres of the Pontic Greeks during the First World War and the Turkish national war; Greece commemorates them on **19 May**. The 1923 exchange brings the survivors to Greece.

The **Επιτροπή Ποντιακών Μελετών** and its journal **Αρχείον Πόντου** start the systematic recording of the dialect. A second wave of Pontic speakers arrives from the former Soviet Union in the 1990s.

head: Feature
Pontic
Standard
rows: Ancient η often kept as [e], not [i]
ω kept as [o] where Koine had ου
No synizesis: ια, ιο → [æ], [ø]; or two syllables
Unstressed ι, ου dropped (like the semi-northern dialects)
Final -ν kept, and added by analogy
Stress can fall 4–5 syllables from the end, with a second stress
long verb forms such as 'we sleep'

head: Feature
Pontic
Standard
rows: Masculine -ος nouns end in -ον, with genitive -ονος
**ο λύκον, τη λύκονος; ο πάππον; ο Τούρκον, τη Τούρκονος**
ο λύκος, του λύκου; ο παππούς; ο Τούρκος
One genitive article **τη** for all genders
του Τούρκου, της γυναίκας, του χωραφιού

head: Feature
Pontic
Standard
rows: Future without an aspect contrast (most areas)
**θα λέγω** = 'I will say' and 'I will be saying'

sections.text: Standard Greek lost the infinitive centuries ago and uses **να** + subjunctive instead (**θέλω να πάω**). The Romeyka of the Trabzon valleys still has an aorist infinitive in **-ίν(ι) / -είν(ι)**: **φαγίνι** 'to eat', **πιείνι** 'to drink', **κόψινι** 'to cut'. Research by Ioanna Sitaridou (Cambridge) shows that it is no longer used freely: it appears only where the event does not happen, after negated past modals, after **πριν** 'before', and in some counterfactuals. Some villages of Sürmene even add person endings to it, an 'inflected infinitive' like the Portuguese one.

examples.el: πριν δοσίνι τα παράν ο Αϊσέ
examples.std: πριν δώσει ο Αϊσέ τα λεφτά

examples.en: if I had said (Sürmene, inflected infinitive)

sections.text: Pontic puts weak pronouns **after** the verb, and uses the **accusative** for every object, direct or indirect (as the northern dialects do). An enclitic **-πα** marks a strongly highlighted topic; Georges Drettas, its main modern describer, links several such word-order features to contact with Turkish.
Pontic keeps many Byzantine and older words, and has borrowed from Turkish above all, but also from Armenian, Georgian, Laz and Kurdish. Some words you will hear at a Pontic **γλέντι**:

sections.h: Romeyka in Turkey and Mariupolitan in Ukraine
sections.el: Ρωμαίικα του Όφη, Ρουμέικα της Μαριούπολης
sections.text:
Muslim villages of the **Of** valley and nearby (Çaykara, Dernekpazarı, Sürmene, Köprübaşı, Tonya) still speak Romeyka, mostly older people. Its speakers are Turkish citizens with Turkish national identity; the dialect keeps archaisms (the infinitive above) alongside many Turkish and Arabic loans. A closely related variety is spoken in **Νέα Τραπεζούντα** in Pieria by descendants of Christians from the same valley.

**Mariupolitan Greek** (**Ρουμέικα**) is spoken in villages north of the Sea of Azov. It continues the Greek of Crimea, once part of the Trebizond world; the Crimean Greeks were resettled around Mariupol by Catherine the Great after 1778. It shares Pontic's lack of synizesis but has northern-type vowel loss. (The Turkic-speaking Greeks of the same area, the **Ουρούμ**, are a different group.)

clips.title: The witches
clips.who: Ioannis Amarantidis, Oinoi (Kastoria). His grandparents came from Matsuka (Maçka) in the hills behind Trabzon. VLACH notes that his Pontic shows influence from written Modern Greek.

cues.el: Εν σον παρχάρ ο πάπον, λίγο τρανίτερος,
cues.tr: En som-barχár o pápon, líɣo traníteros
cues.en: My grandpa was young when he was at the summer pastures,

cues.el: κανά δεκαεφτά δεκαοχτώ χρονών, νέικον παιδί.
cues.tr: kana ðekaeftá ðekaoχtó χronón, néĭkom-beðí.
cues.en: seventeen-eighteen years, a young boy.

cues.el: Έτον σο καλύβ' το βράδ'.
cues.tr: Éton so kalív to vrað.
cues.en: He was in the hut at night.

cues.el: Αυτά που λέω όλοι τα πιστεύαν.
cues.tr: Aftá pu léo óli ta pistévan.
cues.en: Everybody believed these stories.

cues.el: Δηλαδή μπαίνανε στο θυμικό του ανθρώπου
cues.tr: Ðilaðí bénane sto θimikó tu anθrópu
cues.en: They came into the human mind

cues.el: κ' τα βλέπαν κ' τα πιστεύαν.
cues.tr: kʹe ta vlépan kʹe ta pistévan.
cues.en: and they saw them and they believed them.

cues.el: Απού κάποτε εξέβεν οξωκά α σο καλύβ',
cues.tr: Apu kápote ekséven okʃoká a so kalív,
cues.en: After some time, he went out of the hut,

cues.el: με συχωρείς, να κατουρεί.
cues.tr: me siχorís, na katurí.
cues.en: you will excuse me, to pee.

cues.el: Καπινέδες τέτοια δεν είχανε.
cues.tr: Kapinéðes tétĭa ðen íχane.
cues.en: They did not have toilets and things like that.

cues.el: Στα καλύβια όλο το δάσος ελεύθερο.
cues.tr: Sta kalívia ólo to ðásos eléfθero.
cues.en: Next to the huts all the forest was free.

cues.el: Μόλις εξέβεν οξωκά σο καλύβ'
cues.tr: Mólis ekséven okʃoká so kalív
cues.en: He went just out of the hut

cues.el: ακούει απέναντι σο ορμίεν […]
cues.tr: akúi apénandi so ormién […]
cues.en: and there was across the forest

cues.el: στέκ' ένα φως, ένα φωσόπολι
cues.tr: stek éna fos, éna fosópoli
cues.en: a small light,

cues.el: κ' ακούει κ' κεμεντζέν, μουσική δηλαδή.
cues.tr: kʹe akúi kʹe kʹemendʒén, musikʹí ðilaðí.
cues.en: and he heard a pontic lyra – music!

cues.el: «Εγώ πα», λέει, λέει, «ας πάω», λέει, «τηρώ ντο εν εκεκά».
cues.tr: Eɣó pa, leĭ, ʎeĭ, as páo, leĭ, tiró do en ekʹeká.
cues.en: Let’s go to see what is down there.

cues.el: Επήα ως εκεκά. Μόλις α… Λαγγεύ', λέει, το φως,
cues.tr: Epía os ekʹeká. Mólis a. Langʹév leĭ to fos,
cues.en: I went there. The light jumped,

cues.el: πάει απέναντι, κ' ένι μουσική πάλι.
cues.tr: paĭ apénandi kʹ-éni musikʹí páli.
cues.en: it went across and there again I heard music.

cues.el: Τηρώ σο απέναντι πεζ, τραγωδί, λαλία ήτε γυναικείο ήτανε.
cues.tr: Teró so apénandi pez, traɣoðí lalía íte ʝinekʹío ítane.
cues.en: I saw it across from there. There was a song, a woman’s voice.

cues.el: Λέω, θα πάω κ' εκεί.
cues.tr: Léo, θa páo kʹe ekʹí.
cues.en: I said I will go there.

cues.el: Από κάποτε έρθε σο νου μ' ντο ελέν' ατον η καλομάνα.
cues.tr: Apo kápote érθe so nu m do elén-aton i kalomána.
cues.en: Sometime it came into my mind what my grandmother said.

cues.el: Επήα εκεί, λέει, τηρώ, πάλι το ίδιο.
cues.tr: Epía ekʹi, leĭ, teró, páli to íðʝo.
cues.en: I went there, I saw it, again the same.

cues.el: Κ' το φως λαγγεύ' πιο πέρα
cues.tr: Kʹe to fos langʹév pço péra
cues.en: The light jumped, this time further,

cues.el: κ' η μουσική χάνεται για λίγο
cues.tr: kʹe i musikʹí χánete ʝa líɣo
cues.en: and the music was lost for a while,

cues.el: κ' ακούγεται απέναντι.
cues.tr: kʹe akúɣete apénandi.
cues.en: and then it could be heard all across the area.

cues.el: Τότε εθυμέθα κ' λέω: «Ουχ, γλήγορα!»
cues.tr: Tóte eθiméθa kʹe léo. Uχ ɣlíɣora!
cues.en: Then I remembered and said. Oh quickly!

cues.el: Τρέχ', πάει σο καλύβ'.
cues.tr: Treʃ, paĭ so kalív.
cues.en: He ran and went into the hut.

cues.el: Μα, για. Καλομάνα έτσ' κ' αέτσ'.
cues.tr: Ma, ja. Kalomána eʦ kʹ-aéʦ.
cues.en: The grandmother listened to this and that.

cues.el: «Εγώ εσέν κ' είπα σε», λέει.
cues.tr: <Eɣó esén kʹ-ípa se, leĭ.
cues.en: <What did I tell you?

cues.el: «Κι θα πας από πίσ' α σ' αείκα.
cues.tr: Kʹi θa pas apo pis a s-aíka.
cues.en: You will not visit such things.

cues.el: Ατά είναι μάισσες, μάγισσες.
cues.tr: Atá íne máises, máʝises.
cues.en: These are witches. Witches.

cues.el: Θα μαεύνε σε. Άλλη φορά κι θα πας.»
cues.tr: Θa maévne-se. Áli forá kʹi θa pas.>
cues.en: They will bewitch you. You will not go there again.>

cues.el: Ατσέ εποίνε σε αέτσ' η μάισσα:
cues.tr: Aʦé epíne-se aéʦ i máĭsa
cues.en: The witch would do this to you:

cues.el: να πας, πας, πας, μετά θα εμάευες.
cues.tr: na pas pas pas metá θa emáeves.
cues.en: she would chase after you and bewitch you.

cues.el: Δηλαδή θα σ' έπιανε κακό κ' δεν ξέρω τι.
cues.tr: Ðilaðí θa s-épçane kakó kʹe ðen kséro ti.
cues.en: Specifically, a bad person will catch you.

cues.el: Η αλήθεια είναι ότι τα πιστεύανε.
cues.tr: I alíθĭa íne óti ta pistévane.
cues.en: It is true that they believed them.

gloss.σον: σε + τον — in the, to the (Pontic)
gloss.απού: από — from; απού κάποτε, after a while (Pontic)
gloss.α: από — from (Pontic α σο, from the)
gloss.νου: νους — mind; σο νου μ', into my mind
gloss.αέτσ: έτσι — so, like this (Pontic); έτσ' κ' αέτσ', this and that
gloss.κι: κι (Pontic) — not = δεν; elsewhere κι = και 'and'
gloss.πίσ: πίσω — behind; από πίσ' α, after

culture.text: Pontic culture in Greece lives in its music: the **κεμεντζές** (lyra), the **νταούλι** drum, songs about exile and the lost homeland, and line dances such as **σέρρα** and **τικ**. Associations (**σύλλογοι**) in Thessaloniki, Drama, Kozani and Athens teach dances and the dialect, and comedians and singers use it on stage. The **Monastery of Panagia Soumela**, rebuilt in Vermio after 1923 and named after the original near Trabzon, is a pilgrimage site every August 15. On 19 May Greece remembers the Pontic Greeks killed in 1916–1923.

questions.q: In Pontic **νύφε** and **κλέφτες**, what is unusual?
questions.why: Everywhere else η became [i] (νύφη, κλέφτης); Pontic kept an older [e] in many words.

questions.q: **Είπα τον κύρη** shows which Pontic habit?
questions.why: Pontic uses the accusative for all objects; the standard says είπα στον πατέρα / του είπα.

questions.q: Where is the old infinitive still used?
options: In the Romeyka of the Trabzon valleys
In all Pontic spoken in Greece
questions.answer: In the Romeyka of the Trabzon valleys
questions.why: Sitaridou's fieldwork documents forms like φαγίνι, κόψινι, used only in non-realised contexts.

gloss.Πόντος: Πόντος — Pontus, the south-east Black Sea coast
gloss.Ρωμαίικα: ρωμαίικα — 'Roman', i.e. Greek: the speakers' own name for Pontic
gloss.Λαζικά: λαζικά — 'Laz': an older local name for Pontic (not the Kartvelian Laz language)
gloss.Τραπεζουντιακά: Τραπεζουντιακά — the Trebizond group of Pontic dialects
gloss.λύκονος: λύκονος (Pontic) — of the wolf = του λύκου
gloss.Τούρκονος: Τούρκονος (Pontic) — of the Turk = του Τούρκου
gloss.τη: τη (Pontic) — genitive article for all genders = του/της
gloss.γαρής: γαρή (Pontic) — wife, woman; τη γαρής = της γυναίκας
gloss.χωραφί: χωράφι — field; Pontic τη χωραφί = του χωραφιού
gloss.πολλά: πολλά — (Pontic) very; πολλά έμορφος = very beautiful
gloss.λέγω: λέγω — I say (older form of λέω)
gloss.κι: κι (Pontic) — not = δεν; elsewhere κι = και 'and'
gloss.ειπίνα: ειπίνα (Sürmene Romeyka) — (for) me to say: inflected infinitive
gloss.με: με — me (acc.); Pontic λες με = μου λες
gloss.Έγκα: έγκα (Pontic) — I brought = έφερα (from ancient ἤνεγκα)
gloss.σε: σε — you (acc.); Pontic έγκα σε = σου έφερα
gloss.γλέντι: γλέντι — party, festivity with music and dance
gloss.Ουρούμ: Ουρούμ — Turkic-speaking Greeks of Crimea and Mariupol
